questions.q:
Read the statements about the chapter's account of families.
1. A joint family, as the chapter defines it, can include uncles, aunts and cousins as well as grandparents.
2. The chapter says Indian society today has only two types of family.
3. Tamil is given as an example of a language with different terms for an elder and a younger brother or sister.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: 1 and 3 only
o: 1 and 3 only
1 only
2 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q:
A Class 6 group surveys five households in their colony:
H1: a grandmother, her son, his wife and their daughter
H2: a husband, his wife and their son
H3: grandparents, their two sons, the sons' wives and four grandchildren
H4: a father, a mother and their two sons
H5: a couple and their three daughters
(a) Classify each household as joint or nuclear, using the chapter's definitions. (b) Which type is more frequent in this survey, and by how many households? (c) The chapter calls Shalini's household a joint family. If her household were added to the survey, how many joint and how many nuclear households would there be, and would your answer to (b) still hold?
questions.a: (a) H1 joint (three generations), H2 nuclear, H3 joint (three generations with uncles, aunts and cousins), H4 nuclear, H5 nuclear. (b) Nuclear is more frequent: 3 nuclear against 2 joint, so by 1 household. (c) Joint 3, nuclear 3; the two types would be equal, so nuclear would no longer be more frequent.
s: H1 and H3 joint, because several generations live together
H2, H4 and H5 nuclear, as each is a couple and their children
Nuclear more frequent, 3 against 2, by one household
With Shalini's household: 3 joint and 3 nuclear
Conclusion: the types are now equal, so (b) no longer holds

questions.q:
A class lists five households.
(i) A widowed mother and her two sons.
(ii) A couple, their married son, his wife and their baby.
(iii) A father bringing up his daughter alone.
(iv) A couple and their four children.
(v) A grandmother, her daughter-in-law and two grandchildren.
Using the chapter's definitions, the number of these households that are nuclear families is ___.
Rohit argues: 'The chapter says the family is the most ancient unit of society, so the nuclear family must be the oldest type of family.' What is wrong with his reasoning?
questions.a: The chapter never says which type of family is older
o: The chapter never says which type of family is older
The chapter says joint families came after nuclear ones
The chapter says the community is older than the family
The chapter says nuclear families exist only in towns

questions.q:
Selvi, a Tamil speaker, writes to an English pen-friend: 'I have two brothers.' In her Tamil diary she uses two different words for them.
(a) What does each Tamil word tell a reader that the English word 'brother' does not?
(b) Rewrite her English sentence so that it carries the same information as her diary.
questions.a: (a) Whether that brother is older or younger than Selvi; the chapter says Tamil has different terms for an elder and a younger brother or sister. (b) 'I have an elder brother and a younger brother.' English needs extra words ('elder', 'younger') for what one Tamil word carries.
s: Part (a): the Tamil word shows whether the brother is elder or younger
Part (b): a sentence that adds 'elder' and 'younger' to 'brother'

questions.q: The chapter calls the family 'the fundamental and most ancient unit of any society' and, at its end, 'the foundation of human society'. Interpret why the family deserves these titles, giving three ideas from the chapter.
questions.a: 1. Almost all of us live in a family, so nearly everyone's social life starts there. 2. Members of a family ideally support each other in their many duties and tasks, through love, care, cooperation and interdependence. 3. The family is a 'school' where children are raised to become responsible members of society and learn values such as dana, seva and tyaga, so society is built on what families do.
s: Almost everyone lives in a family
Members support each other in duties and tasks
Family raises responsible members of society and teaches values

questions.q: The Joshi household has eight members: a couple and their six children. Priya says, 'With eight people under one roof, it must be a joint family.' Which correction follows the chapter?
questions.a: It is nuclear: the test is who lives there, not how many
o: It is nuclear: the test is who lives there, not how many
It is joint: any home of more than six people is joint
It is neither: a nuclear family has at most four people
It is joint, as the six children are brothers and sisters

questions.q:
Ritu's mother brings her and her brother up alone. Last year Ritu's grandmother (her mother's mother) moved in with them. Ravi says, 'There is only one parent, so the chapter would call it a nuclear family.'
(a) Is Ravi right? Give the chapter's reason.
(b) What change in the household would make his label correct?
questions.a: (a) No. A grandmother, a mother and her children are three generations living together, which the chapter calls a joint family; having one parent does not decide the type. (b) If the grandmother moved out, one parent and her children would remain, which the chapter calls a nuclear family ('sometimes one parent and children').
s: Part (a): not right; three generations living together make it joint
Part (b): the grandmother moving out leaves one parent and children, which is nuclear

questions.q: Compare the way English and Indian languages name family relationships, as described in the chapter, and analyse what the difference reveals about the Indian family. Make five points.
questions.a: 1. English has comparatively few terms to describe family relationships. 2. Indian languages have many more; Hindi, for example, has bua, tau, tai, chacha, mausi, nana, nani and more. 3. Some languages, such as Tamil, even have different terms for an elder and a younger brother or sister. 4. A single word in a mother tongue often needs several words in English: chacha must be put as 'father's younger brother'. 5. Most Indian languages have no word for 'cousin' because cousins are simply 'brothers' and 'sisters'; this richer naming emphasises the deep bonds among all the children in the family.
s: English has few kinship terms
Indian languages have many more, with Hindi examples
Tamil distinguishes elder and younger siblings
One Indian word needs several English words, with an example
No word for cousin, which reveals deep bonds among the children

questions.q:
Tenzing lives with his parents and his grandparents. Suppose his grandparents move to another village to live with Tenzing's father's brother, his wife and their two children.
(a) What type of family would Tenzing's home and his uncle's home each become?
(b) Which words in the chapter's definitions decide the type of Tenzing's home after the move?
questions.a: (a) Tenzing's home: a nuclear family (a couple and their child). His uncle's home: a joint family (grandparents, parents and children, several generations together). (b) A nuclear family is 'limited to a couple and their children'; only his parents and he would remain.
s: Part (a): Tenzing's home nuclear, the uncle's home joint
Part (b): 'limited to a couple and their children' decides Tenzing's home

questions.q: The chapter opens with Tiruvalluvar's line: 'Love and dharma are the flower and fruit of family life.' Link each of the two key words, love and dharma, to one idea the chapter later develops about how a family works.
questions.a: Love: the chapter says relationships among family members are based on love, care, cooperation and interdependence. Dharma: the chapter says following our dharma, or doing our duty, is an important principle of Indian culture, and each family member has a role and responsibility towards the others.
s: Love linked to relationships based on love, care, cooperation and interdependence
Dharma linked to duty and each member's role and responsibility

questions.q: Arjun copies the two examples in the chapter's Hindi table into his notebook, but one of his lines does NOT agree with the table. Which line?
questions.a: Father's elder brother: chacha
o: Father's elder brother: chacha
Mother's brother's daughter: bahan
Father's younger brother: chacha
A cousin who is called a sister: bahan

questions.q: True or False? 'Because most Indian languages have no word for cousin, Indian families must have fewer close relatives than English-speaking families.' Give the verdict and the corrected statement.
questions.a: False. The missing word says nothing about how many relatives a family has. The chapter explains that there is no such word because cousins are treated simply as 'brothers' and 'sisters', which emphasises the deep bonds among all the children in the family.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: cousins are counted as brothers and sisters, showing deep bonds, not fewer relatives

questions.q: Kabir says: 'In a joint family several generations live together, but uncles, aunts and cousins never live in one; they always form their own nuclear families.' Check his claim against the chapter and give your verdict with reasons.
questions.a: Partly right. His first clause is the chapter's own definition: a joint family has several generations living together. His second clause is wrong: the chapter's list of who lives in a joint family includes uncles and aunts, brothers, sisters and cousins, and Shalini's household, with her uncle Chittappa, aunt Chitti and cousin Chinni, is an example. (A verdict of 'No' that credits the first clause as correct and corrects the second earns full marks.)
s: Verdict: partly right
Right part: several generations living together is the chapter's definition
Wrong part: the chapter's joint family includes uncles, aunts and cousins, as in Shalini's home

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Most Indian languages have no separate word for 'cousin'.
Reason (R): Indian languages have fewer words for family relationships than English.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: A is true, but R is false.
o: A is true, but R is false.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: Ananya, who speaks Hindi at home, mentions her 'chacha' in a letter to a pen-pal in London. To make the meaning clear in English she has to write 'my father's younger brother'. Which point of the chapter does this show?
questions.a: One Hindi word may need several English words
o: One Hindi word may need several English words
English has more words for relatives than Hindi does
Chacha is a word that cannot be put into English at all
Hindi has a separate word for every kind of cousin

questions.q:
A school is holding a Family Day. Each pupil ticks one box on a form: 'Joint family (several generations)' or 'Nuclear family (a couple and their children)'. Four entries are received.
Entry W: Tara lives with her grandparents, parents and her father's brother's son.
Entry X: Imran lives with his father and mother and his baby sister.
Entry Y: Kiran's form says 'Joint family'; only her parents and her two brothers live with her.
Entry Z: Joseph lives with his mother and his sister; his mother brings him up alone. He left the form blank.
(a) Which box should Tara tick, and why?
(b) Which entry contains an error, and what is it?
(c) Joseph says neither box fits him. Which box fits him according to the chapter, and what should the school change in the label so that families like his are not left out?
questions.a: (a) Joint family: several generations (grandparents, parents and a cousin) live together. (b) Entry Y: parents and their children only, with no other generation, is a nuclear family, not joint. (c) Nuclear: the chapter says a nuclear family is a couple and their children, and sometimes one parent and children. The label should read 'a couple or one parent, and their children'.
s: Part (a): joint, several generations live together
Part (b): Entry Y is wrong; parents and children only make a nuclear family
Part (c): nuclear, since the chapter includes one parent and children; widen the label

questions.q:
Read this extract from Lakshmi's class report, written in English.
'I live in a big house with my grandparents, my parents, my elder brother, my father's younger brother, his wife and their two sons. At home we speak Tamil. I have three brothers, and I call the eldest of them by a special Tamil word that shows he is older than me.'
(a) Which of Lakshmi's 'three brothers' would an English speaker call her cousins?
(b) According to the chapter, why does she count them as brothers?
(c) The class form, printed in English, asks: 'How many brothers and sisters (not cousins) do you have?' Should Lakshmi write 1 or 3? Justify using the chapter's own example of how a term is put into English.
questions.a: (a) The two sons of her father's younger brother. (b) Most Indian languages have no word for 'cousin', because cousins are simply 'brothers' and 'sisters'; this reflects the deep bonds among all the children in the family. (c) 1. The form uses English terms and itself excludes cousins; the chapter's table shows that in English terms a child of a parent's brother is a cousin (Rani is 'mother's brother's daughter (cousin)'), so only her elder brother counts. In Tamil she would still call all three brothers.
s: Part (a): the two sons of her father's younger brother
Part (b): no word for cousin; cousins are brothers and sisters, showing deep bonds
Part (c): writes 1, because in English terms the uncle's sons are cousins, as the chapter's table shows

questions.q: A survey of 30 households in one colony finds 21 nuclear families and 9 joint families. Which conclusion does the survey support without going against the chapter?
questions.a: In this colony, nuclear families outnumber joint ones
o: In this colony, nuclear families outnumber joint ones
Joint families no longer exist in Indian society today
Nuclear families must be the oldest type of family
Most children in this colony have no cousins at all

questions.q: Write a short description of an imaginary household of at least five members that the chapter would call a joint family. Then name one change of members that would turn it into a nuclear family, and explain why the change works.
questions.a: Sample: Asha lives with her grandparents, her parents and her younger brother (six members, three generations), so it is a joint family. If the grandparents move to another town, only Asha's parents and their two children remain. The household is then limited to a couple and their children, which is the chapter's definition of a nuclear family. (Any household with several generations, and any change that leaves a couple or one parent with their children, earns full marks.)
s: A household of five or more with several generations living together
A change of members that leaves only a couple (or one parent) and children
Explanation using the chapter's definition of a nuclear family

questions.q: Which of these is the LEAST suitable example of tyaga, as the chapter uses the word?
questions.a: An aunt buys herself a new phone with her bonus
o: An aunt buys herself a new phone with her bonus
A father skips new shoes so his daughter can go on a camp
A grandmother gives up her room to a visiting cousin
An elder brother puts off his trip to look after a sick parent

questions.q: A newspaper column says: 'Families today only provide food and shelter; values are learnt only at school.' Would the chapter support this column? Give your verdict with reasons.
questions.a: No. The chapter calls the family itself a 'school', where children learn important values such as ahimsa, dana (giving), seva (service) and tyaga (sacrifice). It says relationships in a family rest on love, care, cooperation and interdependence, not just food and shelter. Children also learn to participate in household life through daily practice and learn traditions followed for generations.
s: Verdict: not supported
The family is a 'school' where children learn values such as dana, seva and tyaga
Relationships rest on love, care, cooperation; children also learn through daily practice and traditions

questions.q: In an imaginary household, each member does only his or her own tasks, never helps anyone else and never gives up anything for another member. Show, using the chapter, why this household could not be described in the chapter's terms of family relationships.
questions.a: 1. The chapter says family relationships rest on cooperation, which it explains as working together, but here nobody works with anyone. 2. It says each member has a role and responsibility towards other members, and growing children take on responsibilities to help other members; here no one helps another. 3. It says individuals often give up their own needs to take care of the family's needs (tyaga); here no one gives up anything. So the household lacks every basis the chapter names.
s: No cooperation (working together)
No responsibility towards or help for other members
No giving up of one's own needs for the family

questions.q:
Mohan says: 'I help my mother cook every evening. The chapter calls this dharma, and dharma means giving things away.'
(a) Correct Mohan's meaning of dharma, and name the value from the chapter's list that does mean giving.
(b) Is helping his mother cook still an example of following dharma? Explain.
questions.a: (a) The chapter explains following one's dharma as doing one's duty; giving is dana. (b) Yes. Helping his mother is doing his duty towards another family member, and the chapter says each member has a role and responsibility towards the others.
s: Part (a): dharma is doing one's duty; giving is dana
Part (b): yes, it is a duty towards a family member

questions.q:
The Mehtas say: 'We want our son to be happy, so he will never do a single chore at home and never have to help anyone.'
(a) The chapter names two things parents are responsible for raising children to become. Which one does the Mehtas' plan leave out?
(b) Using what the chapter says about growing children, suggest one change to their plan.
questions.a: (a) Becoming a responsible member of the society; the plan aims only at a happy individual. (b) As he grows up, let him take on more responsibilities in the home to help other members, for example helping a grandparent or a younger sibling, so that through daily practice he learns to take part in household life.
s: Part (a): the aim of raising a responsible member of society is left out
Part (b): let him take on growing responsibilities that help other members

questions.q: The chapter calls the family a 'school'. In the Kapoor home, the parents do every chore themselves so that the two children can study; the children are given no new jobs at home as they grow older; the family has stopped keeping the customs it followed for generations; nobody at home talks about giving, service or sacrifice; and the grandmother, who used to give up her own wishes for the family, has moved to another city. Identify five lessons of the family 'school' that the Kapoor children may be missing. For each, link the detail in the scene to what the chapter says children learn at home.
questions.a: 1. Chores done for them: through daily practice children learn to participate in the life of the household. 2. No new jobs as they grow: the chapter says that as children grow up they take on more responsibilities in the home to help other members. 3. Customs dropped: in many homes children learn traditions and practices their family has followed for generations. 4. No talk of giving, service or sacrifice: the family is where children learn values such as ahimsa, dana (giving), seva (service) and tyaga (sacrifice). 5. The grandmother gone: the children no longer see a member giving up her own needs to take care of the family's needs, which the chapter says individuals in a family often do.
s: Chores: learning to participate in household life through daily practice
No new jobs: taking on more responsibilities as children grow
Customs dropped: traditions followed for generations
Values such as dana, seva and tyaga not discussed
Grandmother gone: no example of members giving up their own needs for the family

questions.q: Every evening in the Pillai home, nine-year-old Dev fills the water bottles, his sister lays out the plates and their father cooks, so that dinner is ready by eight. Which basis of family relationships does the chapter define in its own words, in a way that describes this scene exactly?
questions.a: Cooperation
o: Cooperation
Love
Care
Strict discipline

questions.q: Compare what parents give to their children with what growing children give back to the family, as the chapter describes them. Then analyse why the chapter calls family relationships interdependent. (3 marks for the comparison, 2 for the analysis.)
questions.a: Comparison: (1) Parents raise their children to become happy individuals and responsible members of society. (2) As children grow up, they take on more responsibilities in the home to help other members, whether parents or a brother or sister. (3) Children also carry the family forward by learning traditions followed for generations, while parents and elders pass them on. Analysis: (4) Each side depends on the other: children need care and upbringing, and the household needs the help growing children give. (5) The chapter therefore bases family relationships on love, care, cooperation and interdependence, with every member holding a role and responsibility towards others.
s: What parents give: raising happy, responsible members of society
What children give: more responsibilities at home as they grow
Traditions passed on by elders and learnt by children
Each side depends on the other
Link to the chapter's basis of interdependence and shared roles

questions.q: Ramesh says that looking after his ageing parents is what he, as their son, ought to do, and he does it without being asked. Which principle, called important in Indian culture by the chapter, is he describing?
questions.a: Following one's dharma, or doing one's duty
o: Following one's dharma, or doing one's duty
Interdependence between two separate communities
Dana, which the chapter explains as giving
A rule made by a Residents' Welfare Association

questions.q:
Read the statements about roles in the family, as the chapter describes them.
1. 'Cooperation' is explained in the chapter as 'working together'.
2. Parents are responsible for raising their children to become happy individuals and responsible members of society.
3. As children grow up, their responsibilities at home become fewer.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: 1 and 2 only
o: 1 and 2 only
2 only
1 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q:
Assertion (A): In the chapter's view, a child who lays the table every evening is learning something, not only helping.
Reason (R): The chapter says that through daily practice children learn to participate in the life of the household.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: Every Sunday Neha carries her elderly neighbour's groceries up four floors, and last month she gave the neighbour's grandchildren her old storybooks. Her friend says, 'Both are dana.' Is the friend right? Explain using the chapter's meanings of dana and seva.
questions.a: Only partly. Giving away the storybooks is dana, which the chapter explains as giving. Carrying the groceries gives nothing away; it is a service done for the neighbour, which is seva (service).
s: The storybooks are dana (giving)
Carrying the groceries is seva (service), not dana

questions.q:
The Rao family keeps a chart of hours spent on home tasks each week.
Member: before / after the mother joined an evening course
Mother: 20 / 8
Father: 6 / 12
Grandmother: 5 / 7
Meera (13 years): 2 / 6
Sunil (8 years): 1 / 2
(a) Find the family's total weekly hours before and after the change, and whose hours rose by the most.
(b) Meera gives up her Saturday art class to cover her extra hours. Which value from the chapter's list does this show?
(c) The mother's hours fell by 12. By how many hours did the other four members' hours rise in all, and which idea from the chapter about each member's role does this show?
(d) The course ends next month. Meera wants to keep six hours. Give one reason from the chapter for letting her, and one fact from the chart the family should weigh first.
questions.a: (a) Before: 20 + 6 + 5 + 2 + 1 = 34 hours; after: 8 + 12 + 7 + 6 + 2 = 35 hours. The father's rose most, by 6 (6 to 12). (b) Tyaga (sacrifice): she gives up her own wish for the family's need. (c) 6 + 2 + 4 + 1 = 13 hours, which more than covers the 12 the mother gave up; each member has a role and responsibility towards the others, so the work is shared (cooperation, interdependence). (d) Reason: the chapter says that as children grow up they take on more responsibilities in the home to help other members. Fact to weigh: Meera's rise of 4 hours was needed only because the mother's hours fell from 20 to 8; when the course ends and the mother's time returns, the family may not need all of Meera's six hours, so they should check whether six still suits her studies.
s: Part (a): 34 before, 35 after; the father up by 6
Part (b): tyaga (sacrifice)
Part (c): 13 hours, shared because each member has a role and responsibility
Part (d): one chapter reason (growing children take on more) and one chart fact (the mother's hours fell only because of the course)

questions.q:
Match each scene (Column A) with the idea from the chapter it shows best (Column B).
Column A
1. A grandmother gives a sack of rice to a neighbour whose crop has failed.
2. A boy spends his evenings nursing his sick grandfather and fetching his medicines.
3. A mother gives up a new saree she wanted so the money can pay her son's school fees.
4. A girl learns the lamp-lighting ritual her family has kept up for many generations.
Column B
a. Seva (service)
b. A family tradition passed down
c. Dana (giving)
d. Tyaga (sacrifice)

In the Bose family, the mother earns the money, the grandfather helps the children with their studies and the children run errands for everyone. When the grandfather fell ill for a month, the children's marks dropped and the mother had to cut her working hours. Which word from the chapter's description of family relationships fits this best?
questions.a: Interdependence
o: Interdependence
Self-sufficiency
Tradition
Cooperation

questions.q:
Two Class 6 pupils list their jobs at home.
Pinky: makes her own bed and packs her own school bag.
Arif: helps his little sister with her spelling and makes tea for his grandfather.
(a) Whose list better fits the chapter's point that growing children take on responsibilities 'to help other family members'? Why?
(b) Add one job to the other pupil's list that would fit the point, and say whom it helps.
questions.a: (a) Arif's: both his jobs help another member (his sister and his grandfather), while Pinky's jobs only look after herself. (b) Sample: Pinky could help her mother wash the utensils after dinner, which helps her mother. (Any job that helps another family member.)
s: Part (a): Arif, because his jobs help other members
Part (b): a job for Pinky that helps another member, naming whom

questions.q: Rina says, 'Cooperation and interdependence are the same thing.' The chapter explains cooperation as 'working together'. Give one family example of members working together on one task, and one example of members depending on each other while doing different tasks. Then say whether the two examples support Rina.
questions.a: Working together: the whole family cleans the house together before a festival. Depending on each other: the mother earns, the grandfather helps the children study, and the children run errands for everyone; each relies on the others though they are not doing the same task. The second example has dependence without working together on one task, so the two words do not mean exactly the same, and Rina is not right. (A verdict such as 'different but overlapping' also earns the mark if it rests on the two examples. Accept any sensible meaning of interdependence, such as members relying on one another.)
s: An example of working together on one task (cooperation)
An example of depending on each other in different tasks, and the conclusion that Rina is not right

questions.q:
Read this extract from Farhan's diary.
'Abba got a bonus of Rs 6,000. Ammi says it will all go into the family savings tin, not on the Rs 3,000 cycle I wanted. I was upset. Then Dadi told me that years ago she sold her gold bangles to pay for Abba's college fees. On Eid, Dadi showed me how to make our sheer khurma, the way her mother taught her and her mother's mother taught her mother.'
(a) Which value from the chapter's list did Dadi show when she sold her bangles?
(b) Which idea from the chapter about what children learn at home does the sheer khurma show?
(c) Abba now suggests buying the cycle and saving the rest of the bonus. What share of the bonus would still be saved?
(d) Should the family accept Abba's suggestion? Decide, weighing the chapter's point that members often give up their own needs for the family's needs against Tenzing's mother's advice about saving.
questions.a: (a) Tyaga (sacrifice). (b) Children learn traditions and practices their family has followed for generations: the recipe has been handed down through several generations. (c) Rs 6,000 - Rs 3,000 = Rs 3,000, which is half of the bonus. (d) Model answer: Yes, accept it. Half the bonus is still saved for unexpected needs, as Tenzing's mother advises, and the chapter says members 'often', not always, give up their own wishes, so meeting one wish of a child does not break the family's sharing. (A 'No' also earns the mark if it weighs both ideas, for example that the family has not yet saved enough for an unexpected need and Farhan can give up his wish for now as Dadi once did.)
s: Part (a): tyaga (sacrifice)
Part (b): traditions followed for generations
Part (c): Rs 3,000, half of the bonus, still saved
Part (d): a decision that weighs giving up needs for the family against saving for unexpected needs

questions.q:
Two cousins read the chapter's line: 'Individuals in the family often give up their own needs to take care of the family's needs.'
Asha: 'This means a good family member must give up everything she wants, all the time.'
Ravi: 'This means family members sometimes put the family's needs before their own.'
Whose reading fits the chapter better? Give reasons.
questions.a: Ravi's. The chapter says 'often', not 'always', so it does not ask members to give up everything all the time. The value it names here is tyaga (sacrifice), shown in the story that follows: Shalini settles for a cotton dress so the whole family, including her uncle's household, can get new clothes, and she is happy about it. She gives up one wish at one time, which is Ravi's 'sometimes', not Asha's 'everything'.
s: Verdict: Ravi's reading fits
The word 'often' does not mean always or everything
Example: Shalini gives up one wish (the silk dress) for the family's need

questions.q: When Kavya was five she only put away her own toys. Now, at eleven, she also helps her younger brother read and reminds her grandmother to take her medicines. Which idea from the chapter does this change show?
questions.a: Growing children take on more home responsibilities
o: Growing children take on more home responsibilities
Parents alone are responsible for every home task
Children learn values only by hearing family stories
Family traditions are followed only on festival days

questions.q: True or False? 'Children learn family values only when their parents sit them down and teach them.' Give the verdict and the corrected statement.
questions.a: False. The chapter says that through daily practice children learn to participate in the life of the household, and in many homes they learn traditions followed for generations; the family itself is a 'school' for values such as dana, seva and tyaga, so values are learnt by living and taking part, not only from lessons given by parents.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: values are also learnt through daily practice and family traditions in the family as a 'school'

questions.q: Interpret why Shalini 'did not mind her simpler dress', giving three points from the story.
questions.a: 1. Her uncle had lost his job and his family could not afford new clothes for Onam, so there was a real need. 2. Acchamma explained to her that this is how families support each other and share what they have. 3. She was happy that everyone in the household could get some new clothes, which mattered more to her than having silk.
s: The uncle's family was in real financial difficulty
Acchamma's explanation about support and sharing
She was happy everyone got new clothes

questions.q:
A group makes this role chart of Tenzing's family for a class display titled 'Families share work and money'.
Father: runs a small grocery store; cleans the house, looks after the vegetable garden and helps the grandmother cook.
Mother: works as a teacher in a nearby school.
Grandmother: tells stories full of humour and wisdom.
Grandfather (row 1): helps Tenzing with his homework and takes him to the school bus stop.
Grandfather (row 2): registers a complaint at the nearby office when the area has a power failure; collected money from the neighbourhood to repair a storm-damaged house.
(a) One row is wrong. Correct it.
(b) Of the rows for the father, the grandmother and the grandfather, which describe help that stays inside the family, and which row describes help that reaches the community?
(c) The display has room for only one more line: either 'Father took on the chores after Mother became busy' or 'Mother says we should always save some money for unexpected needs'. Choose one for this title, and say what the display loses by leaving out the other.
questions.a: (a) The mother's row: she works in a local handicraft cooperative, making traditional fabrics, wood carvings and other items for sale to tourists (the teacher in a nearby school is Shalini's mother). (b) The father's, grandmother's and grandfather's row 1 describe help inside the family; grandfather's row 2 (the power-failure complaint and the neighbourhood collection) reaches the community. (c) Model answer: the saving line, because the chart already shows shared work in the father's row but says nothing yet about money; leaving out the chores line loses the reason why the father's work changed (the mother became busy). (Choosing the chores line also earns the marks if the pupil says it shows work being shared after a change, and that the display then loses the family's planning for money.)
s: Part (a): the mother's row corrected to the handicraft cooperative
Part (b): father, grandmother and grandfather row 1 inside the family; grandfather row 2 reaches the community
Part (c): a choice justified by the title, and what the left-out line would have shown

questions.q: Two pupils compare the stories of Shalini and Tenzing. Which statement is true of BOTH families as the chapter describes them?
questions.a: A grandparent lives in the same home as the child
o: A grandparent lives in the same home as the child
An uncle's family lives in the same home as the child
The mother works in a local handicraft cooperative
A grandparent does social work in the whole colony

questions.q: In Asha's home, the grandmother does all the cooking alone and the grandfather spends the day reading the newspaper. Asha says, 'My home works just like Tenzing's.' Give two ways in which Tenzing's account shows a different sharing of roles.
questions.a: 1. In Tenzing's home the cooking is not left to the grandmother alone: his father often helps her prepare food for everyone. 2. Tenzing's grandfather is active: he helps Tenzing with his homework, takes him to the school bus stop and does social work in the colony.
s: The father helps the grandmother cook
The grandfather helps with homework, the bus stop or social work

questions.q: 'The two family stories show that a family runs on sharing: of money, of work and of wisdom.' Justify this statement with five points, using both stories.
questions.a: 1. Money: Shalini's parents bought new clothes for Chittappa, Chitti and Chinni when her uncle lost his job. 2. Money: Tenzing's parents discuss special expenses together, and his mother wants to save for unexpected needs. 3. Work: Tenzing's father took on cleaning, the vegetable garden and other chores and helps the grandmother cook after his mother became busy. 4. Work: Tenzing's grandfather helps with homework and takes him to the bus stop. 5. Wisdom: Acchamma explained to Shalini that families support each other and share what they have, and Tenzing's grandmother tells stories with humour and wisdom.
s: Sharing money in Shalini's family (clothes for the uncle's family)
Shared money decisions and saving in Tenzing's family
Sharing work: Tenzing's father takes on chores
Sharing work: the grandfather's help with homework and the bus stop
Sharing wisdom: Acchamma's explanation and the grandmother's stories

questions.q: True or False? 'In Tenzing's family, the grandparents are looked after by the others but play no part in bringing Tenzing up.' Give the verdict and the corrected statement.
questions.a: False. Both grandparents help bring Tenzing up: his grandmother tells him stories full of humour and wisdom, and his grandfather helps him with his homework and takes him to the school bus stop.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: grandmother's stories and grandfather's help with homework and the bus stop

questions.q:
Assertion (A): In Tenzing's family, special expenses are discussed by his parents together.
Reason (R): Tenzing's mother says the family should save money only for expenses that have already been planned.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: A is true, but R is false.
o: A is true, but R is false.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: A classmate argues that Tenzing's story shows household chores are meant only for women. Which detail from the story most directly contradicts her?
questions.a: His father cleans, tends the garden and helps cook
o: His father cleans, tends the garden and helps cook
His grandmother tells stories with humour and wisdom
His mother makes fabrics and carvings for tourists
His grandfather reports power failures at an office

questions.q: A drama club is casting grandparents for four new family plays. Which grandparent plays the same role as Tenzing's grandmother?
questions.a: One whose funny, wise tales help children understand people
o: One whose funny, wise tales help children understand people
One who takes the grandchildren to the school bus stop each morning
One who collects money from neighbours after a storm
One who runs the family's small grocery shop by day

questions.q: Mr Sangma, a retired clerk in Shillong, does four things in one week. Which of them is help that reaches beyond his own family, like Tenzing's grandfather's social work?
questions.a: Complains at the office until the lane's streetlight is fixed
o: Complains at the office until the lane's streetlight is fixed
Fetches medicines from the market every day for his own ailing wife
Pays his grandson's school fees after his son's shop closes
Helps his son mend the family roof after a storm

questions.q: A classmate says: 'In a family, each person's jobs are fixed once and for all.' Use what happened in Tenzing's home to give your verdict on this claim.
questions.a: Not supported. When Tenzing's mother became busy in a local handicraft cooperative, his father, who runs a grocery store, joined in cleaning the house, looking after the vegetable garden and other chores, and often helps the grandmother cook. Roles changed when the family's needs changed.
s: Verdict: the claim is not supported
Evidence: the father took on chores after the mother became busy in the cooperative

questions.q: Tenzing's father runs the grocery store. A classmate says, 'He earns, so he should decide special expenses alone. Why does he discuss them with his wife?' Give two reasons from the chapter why the family's way works.
questions.a: 1. Tenzing's mother plans ahead: she says the family should always try to save some money for unexpected needs, so her view guards the family against future trouble. 2. The chapter says family relationships rest on cooperation ('working together') and that members have responsibilities towards each other, so a big decision that affects everyone is made together. (Any other sound reason from the chapter, such as the special expense affecting the whole family, earns the mark.)
s: The mother's planning to save for unexpected needs
Cooperation (working together) and shared responsibility in the family

questions.q: Compare the need each family faced in the two stories and how each family adjusted to meet it. Give three points.
questions.a: 1. Shalini's family faced a need for money: her uncle lost his job, so his household could not buy festival clothes. 2. Tenzing's family faced a need for time and work at home: his mother became busy in the handicraft cooperative. 3. Each family adjusted by sharing: Shalini's parents spread their spending to buy clothes for all, while Tenzing's father took on household chores and helped the grandmother cook. In both, members changed what they did so that the whole family was looked after.
s: Shalini's family: a money need after the uncle's job loss
Tenzing's family: a need for household work after the mother became busy
Both adjusted by sharing money or work

questions.q:
The Lyngdoh family of Meghalaya has four costs this month: rice and vegetables; a school uniform; a Rs 12,000 roof repair after a storm; a family trip to Guwahati.
(a) Using Tenzing's words, which two are basic necessities, and which two are special expenses?
(b) For which costs would Tenzing's parents sit down and talk it over, and which one would his mother's savings be meant for?
questions.a: (a) Basic necessities: rice and vegetables (food) and the school uniform (clothing). Special expenses: the roof repair and the trip. (b) They would discuss the two special expenses together; the roof repair after a storm is an unexpected need, which is what his mother's savings are for.
s: Part (a): food and clothing are basic necessities; the repair and trip are special
Part (b): special expenses discussed together; the repair is an unexpected need met from savings

questions.q:
Read the statements about the two family stories in the chapter.
1. Shalini's father is a teacher in a nearby school.
2. Chitti, Shalini's aunt, is a homemaker.
3. Tenzing's mother makes items for sale to tourists through a local cooperative.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: 2 and 3 only
o: 2 and 3 only
1 and 2 only
3 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q: Neel says: 'Both family stories in the chapter show a member giving up or taking on something so that others in the family are better off.' Is Neel right? Support your verdict with one example from each story.
questions.a: Yes. In Shalini's story, Shalini gives up the silk dress she expected and her parents spend on clothes for Chittappa, Chitti and Chinni so everyone gets new clothes. In Tenzing's story, his father takes on cleaning, the vegetable garden and other chores, and helps the grandmother cook, after his mother becomes busy with the handicraft cooperative.
s: Verdict: right
Shalini's story: the silk dress given up and clothes bought for the uncle's family
Tenzing's story: the father takes on chores when the mother is busy

questions.q: Which conclusion can NOT be drawn from Tenzing's account of his family?
questions.a: His grandfather alone decides the family's spending
o: His grandfather alone decides the family's spending
Elders in the family share in caring for the young child
Housework in his home is shared by men and women
His mother plans ahead for needs that may arise

questions.q:
Shalini's cousin Chinni is drawing her own family tree. Match each person in Shalini's household (Column A) with that person's relation to CHINNI (Column B).
Column A
1. Acchamma
2. Shalini
3. Chitti
4. Shalini's father
Column B
a. her mother
b. her father's mother
c. her father's brother's daughter (cousin)
d. her father's brother

A moral reads: 'A wise family keeps something aside for a rainy day.' (a) Which of the chapter's two family stories contains this idea, and which member voices it? (b) Write a new situation, not taken from the chapter, in which a family acts on this moral and is glad it did.
questions.a: (a) Tenzing's story: his mother says the family should always try to save some money for any unexpected needs that may arise in the future. (b) Sample: The Das family puts Rs 500 a month into a savings box. When their roof leaks badly in the monsoon, they pay for the repair from the box without borrowing. (Any situation with saving beforehand and an unexpected need met later.)
s: Part (a): Tenzing's story
Part (a): his mother, who says to save for unexpected needs
Part (b): a new situation showing saving ahead and an unexpected need met

questions.q: Suppose Acchamma moved out of Shalini's home to live with relatives in another town, and everyone else stayed. Shalini's home would then hold people of ___ generations.

The Nair family lives together: grandfather, parents, two children, and the father's sister. The mother takes a new job and now gets home late, and the same month the father's sister loses her job and cannot pay for her medicines. Using what Tenzing's family and Shalini's family did, suggest five ways the Nairs could cope, using at least one idea from each story, and name the story each idea comes from.
questions.a: Any five, each with its story: 1. The father takes on cleaning, cooking and other chores while the mother is busy (Tenzing). 2. The grandfather helps the children with homework and takes them to the bus stop (Tenzing). 3. The parents discuss the medicine bill, a special expense, together (Tenzing). 4. The family shares its money so the aunt gets her medicines, as Shalini's parents bought clothes for the uncle's household (Shalini). 5. They use money saved earlier for unexpected needs, as Tenzing's mother advises (Tenzing). 6. An elder explains to the children why their own wishes must wait, as Acchamma did with Shalini (Shalini).
s: First way with its story
Second way with its story
Third way with its story
Fourth way with its story
Fifth way with its story, at least one way taken from each story

questions.q:
In a Kolkata home, the family is preparing for Durga Puja. Rupa lives with her parents and younger brother; her uncle, aunt and cousin live with them. Her uncle has just lost his job. The uncle's family has Rs 2,400 saved, kept for the cousin's school fees, which are due at the end of the year. Rupa's parents have Rs 7,000 for festival clothes.
Plan A: Rupa's parents spend Rs 3,500 on a silk dress for Rupa, Rs 1,500 for her brother and Rs 1,000 each for themselves; the uncle's family uses its own savings for its clothes.
Plan B: Rupa's parents spend Rs 1,000 on clothes for each of the seven people in the house.
(a) How many people do Rupa's parents buy for under each plan, and how much less is spent on Rupa's dress under Plan B?
(b) Under Plan A, if the uncle's family spends all its savings equally on its three members, how much does each get, and how does that compare with Plan B?
(c) Plan B follows an idea about families that the chapter shows in Shalini's story. Which idea, and how does Plan B put it into practice here?
(d) Give one reason for each plan, and decide which the family should follow. Either plan can be chosen.
questions.a: (a) Plan A: 4 people; Plan B: 7 people. Rs 3,500 - Rs 1,000 = Rs 2,500 less on Rupa's dress. (b) Rs 2,400 / 3 = Rs 800 each, which is Rs 200 less per person than the Rs 1,000 under Plan B. (c) Families support each other and share what they have, as Shalini's parents bought festival clothes for her uncle's household when he had lost his job; under Plan B Rupa's parents share the same Rs 7,000 so that every one of the seven gets new clothes, and the uncle's family does not have to spend its savings. (d) For Plan A: Rupa gets the dress she hoped for, and the uncle's family still has months to earn back the fees money before the end of the year. For Plan B: the family shares what it has, every member gets clothes of equal value, and the uncle's savings stay untouched while he has no job. Either decision earns the mark if it is backed by a reason that weighs the other plan (for example, Plan A with a note on how the fees will still be met, or Plan B with a word on what Rupa gives up).
s: Part (a): 4 and 7 people; Rs 2,500 less on Rupa's dress
Part (b): Rs 800 each, Rs 200 less than under Plan B
Part (c): families supporting each other and sharing (Shalini's story), applied to Plan B
Part (d): one reason for each plan and a decision that weighs the other plan

questions.q:
Match each scene from village life (Column A) with the reason for coming together, as the chapter gives it, that the scene shows (Column B).
Column A
1. Neighbours cook together for a marriage in one of the homes.
2. The whole hamlet lights lamps together on Diwali night.
3. Families take turns ploughing each other's plots before the rains.
4. An old understanding lets each family cut grass on the common land only after the harvest.
Column B
a. An agreed practice on shared natural wealth
b. Support with agricultural practices
c. Organising a feast or a wedding
d. Celebrating a festival

Kodur village has 40 families. For the wedding of Lakshmi's sister, 16 families lent vessels, 14 cooked the feast and 10 put up the pandal, so every family helped in one way. Last year the same 40 families took turns to help one another harvest paddy.
(a) Which two reasons for coming together, named in the chapter, do these events show?
(b) Lakshmi's cousin says, 'The 40 families are one big joint family.' Correct her, using the chapter's meanings of the two words.
(c) Next month Lakshmi's family is expected to cook at another family's wedding. Which idea in the chapter about members of a community does this show?
(d) For the next wedding Lakshmi's father wants to hire a caterer for Rs 60,000 so that no neighbour has to work. Give one argument for and one against his plan, using the chapter, and decide.
questions.a: (a) Organising feasts, weddings and other events; and supporting each other with agricultural practices such as harvesting. (b) They are a community, a group of connected families and people around them. A joint family is several generations (grandparents, parents, uncles, aunts, cousins) living together in one household; 40 separate households are not one family. (c) A community implies that people do their best to support each other: help given is returned, and families have duties towards the others. (d) For: the neighbours are spared the work and the expense of their time. Against: coming together for weddings and feasts is one of the things that keeps the families of a community connected and supporting one another. Model decision: keep the neighbours' help (perhaps with a smaller paid service), because the help is returned and binds the community. (A decision for the caterer earns the mark if the pupil weighs the loss of coming together.)
s: Part (a): weddings and feasts; support with harvesting
Part (b): a community of connected families, not a joint family living in one household
Part (c): members do their best to support each other; help is returned
Part (d): one argument each way and a justified decision

questions.q: Interpret why the chapter says that shared access to resources 'also means' specific duties for all families and individuals. Give three points.
questions.a: 1. The resources, such as water, grazing lands and forest produce, belong to the whole community, not to one family. 2. The agreed practices on their use provided communities secure access, but they work only if every family follows them. 3. If some families do not do their part, the others suffer, and the chapter says the community will not function smoothly.
s: The resources are shared by the whole community
Agreed practices give secure access only when followed by all
Without duties the community will not function smoothly

questions.q: True or False? 'According to the chapter's idea of community, a person can belong to a community without being related to its other members.' Give the verdict and the reason.
questions.a: True. The chapter says families are connected not only within themselves but also with other families and the people around them, and such a group of connected people may be called a community. So its members include people from other families, not only relatives.
s: Verdict: True
Reason: a community links one's family with other families and people around them

questions.q: A letter to a newspaper says: 'Village common lands and forests are free for anyone to use as they like, whenever they like.' Write the key points of a reply using the chapter. Make four points against the letter and say which part of the letter, if any, has some truth in it.
questions.a: Against the letter: 1. Communities over time agreed upon practices on the use of shared natural wealth such as water, grazing lands and forest produce. 2. These practices, which we may call 'rules', were rarely written down but were followed, so use was not 'as they like'. 3. They provided communities a secure access to resources. 4. Shared access means all families and individuals have specific duties to perform; otherwise the community will not function smoothly. Some truth: 5. The resources are indeed shared, open to all the families of the community rather than owned by one family, but sharing comes with agreed practices and duties.
s: Agreed practices on water, grazing lands and forest produce
Unwritten 'rules' still limit how resources are used
The practices gave secure access to resources
Shared access brings duties, or the community will not function smoothly
Some truth: the resources are shared by the community, but with rules and duties

questions.q: Divya says: 'Agreed practices on the use of water, grazing lands and forest produce are found among many tribal communities, and nowhere else.' Check her claim against the chapter and give your verdict with reasons.
questions.a: Partly right. Her first clause matches the chapter, which says this is the case with many tribal communities. Her second clause is wrong: the chapter adds that, to some extent, it remains the case in village communities in rural India today. (A verdict of 'No' that credits the first clause and corrects the second earns full marks.)
s: Verdict: partly right
Right part: the chapter says this is the case with many tribal communities
Wrong part: also, to some extent, in village communities in rural India today

questions.q: In Pallipadu, families used to help one another with sowing and harvesting, and kept an unwritten understanding that each family cleared the shared irrigation channel in its turn. Over ten years most families stopped both: each now farms alone, and the channel is cleared only when someone feels like it. Analyse the chain of effects on the village, using five ideas from the chapter.
questions.a: 1. Families in a community are connected with other families and people around them; by farming alone they lose one of the ties that made them a community. 2. Support with land preparation, sowing and harvesting is a reason the chapter gives for coming together; without it each family must manage the heavy work by itself. 3. The channel rule was an agreed practice on shared natural wealth (water), a kind of 'rule' though never written down. 4. Such practices gave the community secure access to the resource; when turns are skipped, that secure access to water is lost for everyone. 5. Shared access means every family has specific duties; when they are not done, the chapter says the community will not function smoothly, so the village as a whole suffers, not just the families that stopped.
s: Loss of the connection between families that makes a community
Loss of support with sowing and harvesting
The channel rota was an agreed, unwritten practice on shared water
Secure access to water is lost
Duties not done, so the community does not function smoothly

questions.q:
Assertion (A): An unwritten understanding that no family grazes its cattle on the common field after the rains can be called a 'rule' in the chapter's sense.
Reason (R): The chapter says members of a community come together to celebrate festivals and organise feasts.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: Five families in a hill hamlet help each other at weddings, draw water from one spring and celebrate festivals together. Which term from the chapter best fits this group of five families?
questions.a: A community
o: A community
A joint family
A nuclear family
A cooperative

questions.q:
Read the statements about community in the chapter.
1. The chapter says the word 'community' has a single fixed meaning.
2. In every village, people support each other with land preparation, sowing and harvesting.
3. Agreed practices on shared resources remain, to some extent, the case in village communities in rural India today.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: 3 only
o: 3 only
1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q: Describe an imaginary practice (not from the chapter) by which a village shares one pond. It should fit the chapter's idea of an agreed 'rule' on shared natural wealth and place at least one duty on every family. Then say which feature of your practice makes it a community practice rather than a family one.
questions.a: Sample: In Kothapalli, every family may draw water from the pond for drinking and cattle, but no one may wash clothes in it; in the week before the monsoon, each family sends one person to clear the inlet. Nobody has written this down; the elders and families agreed on it long ago. It is a community practice because many families share the pond and each of them carries a duty, not just one household. (Any practice with shared use, an agreed but unwritten understanding and a duty on every family.)
s: A shared natural resource with an agreed practice on its use
At least one duty placed on every family
Explains that many families share it and carry duties, so it is a community practice

questions.q: Which of these would the chapter NOT give as a reason for the members of a community to come together?
questions.a: Getting a fixed wage for each day they attend
o: Getting a fixed wage for each day they attend
Celebrating a festival and organising a feast
Helping one another with sowing and harvesting
Organising a wedding in one of the families

questions.q: In a village in Telangana, all families graze their cattle on one common field. An understanding, never written down, says every family keeps its herd off the field for a month after the rains. In the chapter's terms, this understanding is best described as:
questions.a: A practice on shared natural wealth, a kind of 'rule'
o: A practice on shared natural wealth, a kind of 'rule'
A law written down and passed by a government office in town
A family tradition kept up inside a single household
A Residents' Welfare Association rule for a colony

questions.q:
A school cricket team has boys from eight different villages who meet only for practice and matches.
(a) Which of the chapter's examples of a community does the team match better: connected families and the people around them, or a group with a common interest such as 'our school's art community'?
(b) Give the detail about the team that decides your answer.
questions.a: (a) A group with a common interest, like a school's sports community. (b) The boys are linked by the game they play together, not by their families being connected and living around one another (they come from eight different villages).
s: Part (a): a common-interest community
Part (b): linked by the game, not by connected neighbouring families

questions.q:
In a Wardha village, the Patil, Shaikh and Bhosale families take turns to sow and harvest one another's cotton fields.
(a) Is this coming together within a family or within a community? Give the chapter's reason.
(b) The Patils' own sons and daughters also work on the Patil field. Does that part show the same thing? Explain.
questions.a: (a) Within a community: different families support each other with sowing and harvesting, which the chapter gives as a reason why village communities come together. (b) No. That is members of one family working inside their own family; a community is the connection between one family and other families and people around it.
s: Part (a): community, as different families support each other with farm work
Part (b): no, that is help within one family

questions.q:
In a forest hamlet of 25 families, an old unwritten understanding allows each family to gather at most 4 baskets of sal leaves a week from the common forest. A trader offers Rs 30 a basket for 50 extra baskets a week. Ten families want to gather 5 extra baskets each to fill the order; the other 15 families say the forest cannot spare more.
(a) How many baskets a week does the whole hamlet gather under the understanding?
(b) If the ten families went ahead, by what percentage would the hamlet's weekly gathering rise, and how much extra would each of the ten earn a week?
(c) Why, in the chapter's terms, should the ten families not simply go ahead on their own?
(d) Should the hamlet as a whole agree to change its practice for the order? Give one point for and one against, and decide.
questions.a: (a) 25 x 4 = 100 baskets. (b) 10 x 5 = 50 extra, which is 50 / 100 = 50% more; each family earns 5 x Rs 30 = Rs 150 a week. (c) The practice was agreed upon by the community and gives everyone secure access; every family has duties under it, and if some break it the community will not function smoothly. (d) For: the ten families would earn Rs 150 a week each. Against: the practice gives the whole community secure access to the forest, and 15 families fear the forest cannot spare 50% more. Model decision: no, or only a smaller change agreed by all, because the practice belongs to the whole community. (A 'yes' earns the mark only if it is a change agreed by the whole community and weighs the risk to secure access.)
s: Part (a): 100 baskets a week
Part (b): 50% more; Rs 150 a week each
Part (c): the practice is agreed by the community, gives secure access and places duties on all
Part (d): one point each way and a decision for the whole community

questions.q:
A village keeps three agreed practices: (i) no family cuts green branches in the village grove; (ii) each household draws only two pots a day from the spring in summer; (iii) cattle stay off the common pasture until the grass grows back.
(a) Match each practice to the kind of shared natural wealth the chapter names.
(b) Which practice matters most to a family that keeps goats, and what duty does it place on that family?
questions.a: (a) (i) forest produce; (ii) water; (iii) grazing lands. (b) Practice (iii): the goat-keeping family depends on the common pasture, and its duty is to keep its goats off the pasture until the grass has grown back.
s: Part (a): forest produce, water and grazing lands matched
Part (b): the pasture practice, with the duty of keeping the goats off until the grass regrows

questions.q: A pupil says, 'A joint family of 15 people living in one house is a community, because it is so large.' Which reply follows the chapter?
questions.a: It is a family; a community links it with other families
o: It is a family; a community links it with other families
It is a community, because any group of ten or more is one
It is a community, because its members share duties
It is neither, because a family must be a nuclear one

questions.q: A pupil says the agreed practices on shared resources described in the chapter belong only to the distant past. Which point from the chapter answers her?
questions.a: They remain, to some extent, in rural India today
o: They remain, to some extent, in rural India today
They remain in full force in every village today
They were replaced by written laws in all villages
They survive only among tribal communities today

questions.q: On Pongal, the Raman household (grandparents, parents and children) cooks pongal together at home; in the evening the whole street holds a shared feast. Which part of the day shows family and which shows community? Give the feature from the chapter that decides each.
questions.a: Family: the Raman household cooking at home, as several generations living together form one family, with members sharing roles. Community: the street feast, because families connected with other families and people around them come together to celebrate festivals and organise feasts.
s: Family: the household cooking at home, one family of several generations
Community: the street feast, connected families coming together for a festival

questions.q:
Read the statements about the two examples in the chapter's DON'T MISS OUT box.
1. The halma tradition is about coming together to support only the richest families in times of crisis.
2. During the Chennai floods of 2015, almost all shops were closed.

'GREENFIELD RESIDENTS' WELFARE ASSOCIATION. From 1 July: (1) Wet and dry waste must be kept in separate bins for collection. (2) Maintenance is Rs 900 a month per flat. Residents participate in making RWA rules
